summary:
Raconteur argues enterprise AI is entering a "second act" that shifts from automation to augmentation. Many leaders cut hiring or headcount after adopting generative AI, assuming routine work could be automated. Two years on, the piece says that assumption was only partly right: AI makes generating text and code nearly free, but verifying output still requires experienced human judgement, which is expensive and now the scarce resource rather than computation.

Evidence cited includes SAP and Oxford Economics research: UK businesses report average annual AI returns of 2.7 million pounds and expect investment to rise 40% over the next two years, yet only 7% have a comprehensive enterprise-wide AI strategy and 60% say employees lack adequate AI training.

Case examples: Klarna pursued an AI-first strategy and shrank its workforce through natural attrition, later acknowledging the approach prioritised cost over quality and reinvesting in human customer support. Lloyds Banking Group plans to recruit more than 1,000 AI specialists and is expanding workforce development via its AI Academy, reflecting demand for engineers, data scientists and AI governance specialists. At Standard Chartered, CEO Bill Winters sparked debate over AI-driven workforce change before reaffirming commitment to reskilling; chief strategy and talent officer Tanuj Kapilashrami wrote on LinkedIn that businesses must focus on employability rather than just employment, and predicted new global hubs for "hot skills" beyond traditional financial centres.

The piece closes with a pipeline warning: entry-level roles are where future managers, engineers and specialists build professional judgement. If AI absorbs too much of that early work, organisations may face a shortage of experienced professionals able to verify increasingly autonomous systems. Competitive advantage, it concludes, will come from knowing who and what to trust rather than generating more output.

No workplace, facilities, visitor management or hybrid attendance content appears in the item.
